question_text: What is a constellation?
choices: A named pattern or area of stars in the sky
A group of planets tied together
A cloud that circles Earth
A picture made by connecting the Moon's craters
correct_answer: A named pattern or area of stars in the sky
explanation: People use constellation names to find and talk about patterns and regions of stars in the night sky.
traps: Thinking a constellation is a real shape made by stars connected together.

question_text: Are the stars in a constellation usually close together in space?
choices: Not necessarily; they can be very far apart from one another
Yes; they touch each other
Yes; they are all the same distance from Earth
No; they are only dots painted on a screen
correct_answer: Not necessarily; they can be very far apart from one another
explanation: A constellation is a pattern we see from Earth. Its stars can be at very different distances from us and from each other.
traps: Thinking stars that look close must be neighbors in space.

question_text: Which constellation is easy to recognize by three bright stars in a row called Orion's Belt?
choices: Orion
Scorpio
Aquarius
Aries
correct_answer: Orion
explanation: Orion is a well-known constellation. Three bright stars in a row form the part called Orion's Belt.
traps: Thinking the three belt stars are a separate planet or constellation.

question_text: What is the Big Dipper?
choices: A star pattern that is part of the larger Ursa Major constellation
A planet with a handle
A group of seven moons
A spacecraft that visits Jupiter
correct_answer: A star pattern that is part of the larger Ursa Major constellation
explanation: The Big Dipper is an easy-to-spot pattern of stars within the larger constellation Ursa Major.
traps: Calling the Big Dipper a constellation on its own in every star map.

question_text: In the Northern Hemisphere, which star is close to the direction of north in the sky?
choices: Polaris, the North Star
Sirius
Betelgeuse
The Sun
correct_answer: Polaris, the North Star
explanation: Polaris appears close to the north celestial pole, so it can help people find north in the Northern Hemisphere.
traps: Thinking Polaris is the brightest star in the night sky.

question_text: Why do different constellations appear in the evening sky at different times of year?
choices: Earth orbits the Sun, so nighttime points toward different parts of space
The stars turn on and off with the seasons
The constellations move around Earth once a month
The Moon carries the stars to new places
correct_answer: Earth orbits the Sun, so nighttime points toward different parts of space
explanation: As Earth travels around the Sun, the night side faces different directions in space during the year.
traps: Thinking the stars quickly move around Earth or disappear in summer.

question_text: Are the lines people draw between stars in a constellation really in the sky?
choices: No; the lines are imaginary guides people use to show a pattern
Yes; they are glowing ropes
Yes; they are trails left by rockets
No; the stars are not real
correct_answer: No; the lines are imaginary guides people use to show a pattern
explanation: Stars are real, but the lines connecting them are drawn on maps or imagined by stargazers.
traps: Believing the stars are physically joined by bright lines.

question_text: What do zodiac constellations have in common?
choices: They lie near the path the Sun seems to follow through the sky during the year
They are all visible every night
They are the closest stars to Earth
They are planets that orbit the Moon
correct_answer: They lie near the path the Sun seems to follow through the sky during the year
explanation: As Earth orbits the Sun, the Sun appears against different background constellations along a yearly path.
traps: Thinking the Sun really travels around Earth through the stars.

question_text: How are stars different from planets?
choices: Stars make their own light; planets mostly reflect a star's light
Planets make all the light in space
Stars are made of rock and have oceans
There is no difference
correct_answer: Stars make their own light; planets mostly reflect a star's light
explanation: A star like the Sun produces light and energy. A planet usually looks bright because it reflects starlight.
traps: Thinking every bright object in the sky is a star.

question_text: What can a star's color tell astronomers?
choices: Its surface temperature; blue stars are hotter than red stars
How many planets it has for sure
Its exact distance from Earth
Whether it has a name
correct_answer: Its surface temperature; blue stars are hotter than red stars
explanation: A star's color gives clues about its surface temperature. Blue-white stars are hotter than red stars.
traps: Assuming a red star is hotter because red things can look hot on Earth.

question_text: What is the Milky Way?
choices: The galaxy that contains our Sun and solar system
A white cloud around Earth
A ring around the Moon
The name of our Sun
correct_answer: The galaxy that contains our Sun and solar system
explanation: Our Sun is one of the many stars in the Milky Way galaxy.
traps: Confusing the Milky Way galaxy with the solar system.

question_text: Which is bigger: our solar system or the Milky Way galaxy?
choices: The Milky Way galaxy
Our solar system
They are the same size
The Moon is bigger than both
correct_answer: The Milky Way galaxy
explanation: The solar system is one tiny part of the Milky Way, which contains many billions of stars.
traps: Thinking our solar system includes all the stars in the galaxy.

question_text: What does a light-year measure?
choices: A very large distance
How bright a star is
How long a day lasts on Earth
How hot the Sun is
correct_answer: A very large distance
explanation: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year. It is a way to measure the huge distances between stars.
traps: Thinking a light-year is a measure of time because it contains the word 'year'.

question_text: What is a black hole?
choices: A place in space where gravity is so strong that even light cannot escape from inside its boundary
A hole drilled through a planet
A dark cloud that eats stars with teeth
A planet with no sunlight
correct_answer: A place in space where gravity is so strong that even light cannot escape from inside its boundary
explanation: A black hole is an object with extremely strong gravity. From inside its event horizon, not even light can escape.
traps: Thinking black holes are empty holes that travel around space.

question_text: What is a supernova?
choices: A powerful explosion that can happen when a star reaches the end of its life
A new planet being born in one second
A storm on Earth
A small comet with a bright tail
correct_answer: A powerful explosion that can happen when a star reaches the end of its life
explanation: Some stars end their lives in enormous explosions called supernovas, which spread material into space.
traps: Thinking a supernova is a kind of planet or ordinary solar flare.

question_text: What is a comet mostly made from?
choices: Ice, dust, and rocky material
Only liquid water
Hot gas like the Sun
Wood and metal
correct_answer: Ice, dust, and rocky material
explanation: Comets are small bodies made of icy material mixed with dust and rock.
traps: Thinking a comet is a star because it can look bright.

question_text: Why can a comet grow a glowing cloud and tail when it comes near the Sun?
choices: The Sun warms its ice, releasing gas and dust
The comet catches fire like a log
The Moon blows air onto it
It grows a tail made of stars
correct_answer: The Sun warms its ice, releasing gas and dust
explanation: As the comet warms, gas and dust escape from it and form a cloud and tails pushed away from the Sun.
traps: Thinking a comet's tail is a flame or always trails behind its motion.

question_text: What is an asteroid?
choices: A small rocky or metallic object that orbits the Sun
A star that has gone dark
A cloud floating in Earth's sky
A planet's shadow
correct_answer: A small rocky or metallic object that orbits the Sun
explanation: Asteroids are rocky or metallic bodies that orbit the Sun. Many are found in the main asteroid belt.
traps: Mixing up asteroids with meteors, which are streaks of light in our atmosphere.

question_text: Where is the main asteroid belt?
choices: Between Mars and Jupiter
Between Earth and the Moon
Inside the Sun
Between Mercury and Venus
correct_answer: Between Mars and Jupiter
explanation: The main asteroid belt is a region of many rocky objects between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
traps: Confusing the main asteroid belt with the icy Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune.

question_text: What is a shooting star?
choices: A streak of light made when a small space rock heats up in Earth's atmosphere
A star falling from the sky
A comet landing on the Moon
A planet moving across the Sun
correct_answer: A streak of light made when a small space rock heats up in Earth's atmosphere
explanation: A shooting star is a meteor: the light made when a small space object travels through Earth's atmosphere.
traps: Thinking a real star has fallen out of the sky.

question_text: Why can we see many meteors during a meteor shower?
choices: Earth passes through a trail of small bits of dust and rock in space
Stars fall toward Earth in groups
The Moon throws rocks into the atmosphere
Clouds make sparks at night
correct_answer: Earth passes through a trail of small bits of dust and rock in space
explanation: When Earth crosses a stream of debris left by a comet or asteroid, many tiny pieces make meteors in the atmosphere.
traps: Thinking meteor showers are caused by actual stars falling.

question_text: What do scientists call a space rock that makes it through the atmosphere and lands on Earth?
choices: A meteorite
A comet
A constellation
A solar flare
correct_answer: A meteorite
explanation: A space rock is a meteoroid in space, a meteor when it makes a streak in the air, and a meteorite if a piece reaches the ground.
traps: Using the words meteoroid, meteor, and meteorite for the same stage.

question_text: Is the Milky Way the only galaxy in the universe?
choices: No; the universe contains many galaxies
Yes; all other stars are in our solar system
Yes; the Milky Way is the whole universe
No; galaxies only exist in stories
correct_answer: No; the universe contains many galaxies
explanation: The Milky Way is our home galaxy, and there are many other galaxies spread across the universe.
traps: Confusing the Milky Way galaxy with the entire universe.

question_text: What keeps the stars and gas in a galaxy moving together as a huge system?
choices: Gravity
Wind from Earth
Strings between the stars
The Moon's light
correct_answer: Gravity
explanation: Gravity acts across the enormous galaxy and helps hold its stars, gas, and other material together.
traps: Imagining a galaxy is held together by a solid shell.

question_text: When we see light from a very faraway star, what can be true?
choices: The light may have started traveling toward us a long time ago
The light arrives before the star makes it
The star must be inside Earth's atmosphere
The star is always younger than the light
correct_answer: The light may have started traveling toward us a long time ago
explanation: Light takes time to travel through space, so distant stars are seen as they were when the light began its journey.
traps: Thinking we see distant stars exactly as they are right now.
